title: The 2026 Enterprise Guide to Agentic Process Automation
summary: Use an insurance eligibility workflow to explore where APA fits, how to evaluate platforms, and what it takes to move into production.
body_markdown:
Agentic process automation (APA) uses AI agents to plan and execute business workflows. You define the goal, the information available, and the rules the agent must follow. The agent then interprets what it encounters, chooses its next actions, and works toward the result, with human review where needed.


At Skyvern, we build and maintain a[browser automation platform](https://github.com/Skyvern-AI/skyvern?ref=skyvern.com) that combines computer vision and AI to interpret web pages and interact with them. It can navigate websites, fill forms, download documents, and extract information, helping teams automate work in systems that don’t offer a suitable API of their own.


In this guide, I’ll explain which enterprise workflows suit APA, how to evaluate a platform, and what it takes to move from a pilot to production.


We’ll follow an insurance eligibility workflow to make those decisions concrete, then work through the costs, controls, and steps for planning your first deployment.


*If you'd rather skip the long explanation and see what Skyvern can do for your specific use-case, we'd be happy to*[setup a personalized demo with your exact use-case](https://meetings.hubspot.com/skyvern/demo?ref=skyvern.com) *.*


## 1. What is agentic process automation?


Agentic process automation uses AI agents to carry out business processes within a defined scope. An agent receives an objective, observes the available information, chooses an action, and checks what happened before continuing.


For an eligibility check, the objective is to find a member's coverage status for a specified date and return the relevant information. The workflow also needs boundaries: which account it can use, which records it may access, and when it should stop for review.


Agents can work through APIs, browsers, and other tools. Browser automation is especially relevant when the required work is available through a website and there is no suitable API connection.


### How APA fits alongside RPA and APIs


The useful comparison is how much of the execution path you can define in advance.


Approach


Where to consider it


What to evaluate


API integration


The systems expose the operations and data you need through supported APIs.


Coverage, permissions, version changes, and error handling.


RPA or scripted UI automation


The steps are well understood and the application is sufficiently predictable.


How elements are identified, how exceptions are handled, and who maintains the workflow.


Agentic automation


The objective is clear, but completing it requires interpreting information or choosing actions during execution.


Decision accuracy, operating boundaries, cost, and recovery when the agent cannot proceed.


These approaches can coexist. An agent might navigate a portal, a rule might validate the result, and an API might update the destination system.


## 2. Which enterprise workflows are a good fit?


A good way to identify enterprise workflows suited to APA is to look at where your team spends time repeating the same tasks across websites and systems. Prioritize work with a clear result you can verify, such as downloading the right invoice or checking a member’s coverage status.


Her eare some simple examples, taken from real use-cases our clients use Skyvern for:


Workflow


A useful first scope


Result to capture


Healthcare eligibility verification


Check coverage for a defined set of members on one payer portal.


Coverage information, the date checked, and exceptions requiring review.


Insurance operations


Retrieve claim or policy status from a carrier portal.


The status shown, its reference number, and supporting evidence.


Procurement and finance


Download invoices for one vendor and billing period.


The correct documents, invoice identifiers, and missing items.


Government and legal administration


Prepare an application or check a filing's status.


A draft ready for review, a status record, or a submission receipt where submission is authorized.


A good first candidate has inputs you can supply consistently and an output someone can verify. It also has a clear owner who understands the exceptions.


Be more cautious when the process itself is unsettled. If experienced staff disagree about the correct outcome, clarify the policy before asking an agent to execute it. Likewise, if a supported API or a simple rule already covers the work reliably, include that option in the comparison.


Keep the initial scope manageable. One portal and one type of eligibility check provide a clearer test than an attempt to automate every payer and every exception at once.


## 3. How an APA workflow runs


An APA workflow uses the information you provide to complete a task. For example, it can use a member ID, insurer, and date of service to check coverage in a portal and return the result to your system.


Here is a quick overview of a typical APA workflow to retrieve coverage information:


1. Provide the member details and define what the agent can access or change.
2. Sign in to the portal and find the relevant record. Stop or request help if login fails.
3. Read the coverage information and flag any missing details.
4. Check that the result matches the member and date requested. Send unclear or conflicting information to a person for review.
5. Return verified results to your system, flag unresolved cases, and keep a record of the run.


A completed run still needs a usable result. For example, “member not found” means the lookup finished, but the eligibility check needs follow-up.


## 4. What you need before production


A useful pilot tests more than whether an agent can complete a straightforward example. It should establish what happens when the portal behaves differently, the input is incomplete, or someone needs to intervene.


### Authentication and access


Document how the workflow signs in, receives verification codes, and responds when a session expires. Test those paths using the accounts and authentication methods intended for deployment.


Keep access limited to the work the agent needs to perform. Agree who can change credentials and workflow settings, and decide how sensitive information is handled in screenshots, recordings, and logs.


For the eligibility example, a login failure should produce a visible exception. It should not leave the receiving system treating an old result as a fresh check.


### Review and recovery


Choose review points based on the consequence of an incorrect action. Looking up a status and submitting a filing need different controls.


A reviewer should receive the request, the information collected so far, the reason for escalation, and the action awaiting a decision. Define what happens if nobody responds within the allowed time.


Recovery also needs explicit rules. If a run stops after submitting a form, check whether the portal accepted it before retrying. If a session expires during a lookup, decide whether the workflow can safely restart and how to record the interruption.


Browser state, saved application data, and a completed business action are different things. Verify which of them a recovery mechanism preserves.


### Records and ownership


Keep enough information to investigate a result: the original request, execution times, actions taken, returned values, and any review decisions. Set access and retention rules appropriate to the information involved.


Assign an owner for failed runs and a route for reporting recurring problems. Decide who changes the workflow when the portal or business process changes.


These decisions give a pilot a route into daily operations. They also expose work that belongs in the implementation budget, such as building a review queue or connecting results to an existing system.


## 5. How to evaluate an APA platform


Ask vendors to demonstrate the process you intend to automate, including the parts that are difficult today. Use representative inputs and include known exceptions in the evaluation.


Area


What to test


Evidence to inspect


Navigation


Different page states and layouts within your intended scope.


Recordings showing the actions taken and the final page reached.


Authentication


Your actual login and verification methods, including an expired session.


Successful sign-ins, visible failures, and the configured recovery path.


Output accuracy


Missing fields, ambiguous matches, and records with similar identifiers.


Results checked against the source and routed correctly when uncertain.


Human review


A case that needs a decision before continuing.


The information the reviewer receives and what happens after their response.


Recovery


An interrupted lookup or an uncertain submission outcome.


A controlled restart or escalation without duplicate business actions.


Operations


Repeated runs at a representative volume.


Completion times, costs, failure reasons, and staff effort.


Agree on success criteria before the evaluation starts. Useful measures include the percentage of results accepted without correction, the percentage requiring review, time per completed case, and cost per accepted result.


Check the denominator behind each metric. A completion rate can be misleading if it excludes difficult cases or counts technically finished runs whose outputs were unusable.


Also inspect how much work it takes to make a change. Ask the person who would own the automation to update a field, adjust a rule, and diagnose a failed run during the trial.

Start with your own baseline: transaction volume, staff time, errors requiring rework, and the cost of maintaining existing automation.

## 7. How Skyvern supports the workflow


Skyvern automates work in a browser, including signing in, filling forms, downloading files, and extracting data. Teams can build agents in the app or use its APIs and SDKs to connect browser work to other systems.


For the eligibility example, a workflow can combine a Login block, browser actions, structured extraction, validation, and a[Human Interaction block](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/reference/blocks) where review is required. Configure and test these components against the chosen portal.


[Authentication setup](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/credentials) depends on how the portal delivers verification. Skyvern can generate authenticator codes from a stored key. Email codes can come from a connected inbox or be supplied to the run. SMS codes can be pushed to Skyvern through an integration or entered manually. Confirm the complete delivery path during the pilot.


Skyvern also supports[combining AI actions with selectors](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/developers/browser-automation) and replaying successful workflows as cached code with AI fallback. This gives teams options for using predictable steps where they work and agent behavior where the page requires interpretation.


When a run needs investigation, you can[inspect its timeline, screenshots, recording, and outputs](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/cloud/runs) to understand what happened. Use those records to assess errors and refine the workflow.


### For developers: trigger a configured workflow


This integration example assumes you have already built and tested a workflow with inputs named` login` and` member_id` . Its authentication, extraction, and review rules live in the workflow configuration. The member identifier below is a test value.


```text
import asyncio
import os


from skyvern import Skyvern


async def main():
skyvern = Skyvern(api_key=os.environ["SKYVERN_API_KEY"])


run = await skyvern.run_workflow(
workflow_id=os.environ["ELIGIBILITY_WORKFLOW_ID"],
parameters={
"login": os.environ["PAYER_CREDENTIAL_ID"],
"member_id": "TEST_MEMBER_001",
},
wait_for_completion=True,
)


if run.status != "completed":
raise RuntimeError(
f"Run {run.run_id} ended with status {run.status}"
)


print(f"Completed run: {run.run_id}")


asyncio.run(main())


```


The parameter names must match your configured workflow. The returned` run.output` contains the workflow's output, which your integration should validate before using it downstream. The[Python SDK reference](https://www.skyvern.com/docs/sdk-reference/agents) documents the call and response fields.


## 8. Plan your first pilot


Choose a workflow small enough to inspect closely and useful enough that success would change someone's working day.


For an eligibility pilot, that could mean one payer portal, one type of check, and a defined set of cases. Name an operations owner and agree where the results will go.


Then work through five steps:


1. Measure the current process. Record time per case, rework, and the exceptions staff encounter.
2. Define an acceptable result. Specify required fields, accuracy checks, review conditions, and actions the workflow may take.
3. Build the full path. Include authentication, result delivery, monitoring, and escalation in the pilot scope.
4. Test representative cases. Include missing information, failed logins, ambiguous results, and interruptions alongside straightforward checks.
5. Review the evidence before expanding. Compare accepted results, staff effort, cost, and recovery behavior with the baseline. Address recurring failures before adding portals or volume.


Bring a workflow, a sample of its exceptions, and the output your team needs to a[Skyvern demo](https://meetings.hubspot.com/skyvern/demo?ref=skyvern.com) . That gives the discussion a concrete starting point and a result you can evaluate.
